cells.tense: You are the one laying out the categories right now, and you know it.
cells.ask: Show someone the layout you're already running — the shelves, the labels, the order you file things under. Then leave it with them unedited.
cells.core:
You're the one drawing the lines, and you can feel it as you do it. Things arrive loose and you find the shape under them — what belongs with what, what has to come before what else. You file life in a way you can reach into, and the filing holds.

The balance has a price and you're paying it. Every structure you set down makes some things easy and some things impossible, and you aren't pretending otherwise. What keeps this clean is how you hold the people in it: you can see someone recognize the layout you've made and not need them to live inside it the way you do.
cells.sheetLine: You draw the lines, and you know you're drawing them.
cells.verb: finding the pattern in what's scattered and building it into something that holds
cells.place: where the architecture gets decided — the shape a piece of life is filed under

cells.tense: You are bracing for a future that isn't here and can't be written in.
cells.ask: Pick one thing already fully shaped. Leave one part of it deliberately open. Don't fill it in when the unease arrives — let it stand as it is.
cells.core:
The analysis has outrun what it's analyzing. You're already sorting next month, building a frame for a thing that hasn't taken its final size, and the frame is crowding the thing itself. The wish under it is that if the structure is tight enough, nothing arrives that can't be filed. Logic at that pitch starts to rule instead of serve.

Between the certainty and the grip there's nothing solid left to stand on. So take one piece that's finished and usable, and leave a gap you'd normally seal. Whatever grabs at you to close it is the structure talking, not the work.
cells.sheetLine: You've built the frame bigger than the thing it holds.
cells.verb: finding the pattern in what's scattered and building it into something that holds

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that shut behind you.
cells.ask: Take one small mess you've been leaving alone. Sort it into three piles and decide only where the piles go. Nothing beyond that today.
cells.core:
The lines went soft and stayed that way. You can see where things should sit, you know the pattern, and you don't put it down — everything stays in one loose pile because sorting it means saying what belongs with what, and that call is the one that stopped happening. The ability is intact. The move toward it isn't.

You can't build this one by thinking harder. Take a small heap that costs you little, and start naming where the pieces should land. Say which pile is which out loud, low stakes, no audience, and let that be the whole job for today.

cells.tense: The pen is down, and you're still writing in this room every day.
cells.ask: Pick one arrangement around you that others rely on. Say out loud that you made it, without naming it as the thing or the system.
cells.core:
People keep working inside a shape you made. The schedule, the labels, the way a thing gets split and handed out — you drew all of it, and you talk about it like it arrived by itself. When it's working, this is structure that carries what it holds: clear enough that things simply make sense in the room you're standing in. The author has stepped out and the structure keeps running without the credit.

Notice the moment someone says it works, and what moves in you before you hand the credit to anyone. The recognition you're scanning for starts with a plain claim. One arrangement in reach is yours, and it's worth hearing yourself call it that, to someone who can hear you.

attempts.check: The record does not say what the person's structure is for at work, who reads what they build, or how fast it has to ship, so nothing in any cell should locate a deadline, a team, or a history. A reader could reasonably say the structure that once worked is no longer wanted, or that the tightening isn't happening and the looseness is. The ask in each cell stands on its own as one visible act, useful even if the read misses. The sentence that would serve the writer more than the person is any line about order arriving just in time, and none of it appears. Too Little and Too Much are written as the same capacity starved and overdriven: the container made and the container swollen to hold everything before it happens.
